comparator.name: European Public Health
comparator.sourceNotes: The 2026–2027 regulations specify a 150 EC major and a 30 EC approved minor. The final year includes a 6 EC thesis proposal and a 30 EC placement and individual thesis.
components: Health, Health Determinants and the European Union (EPH1021)
Communicable and Non-communicable Diseases in the EU and WHO-Euro (EPH1022)
Introduction to Academic Writing and Year 1 Paper (EPH1027)

Health Technological Innovation and EU Legal Competencies (EPH1025)
Introduction to Statistical Methods for Data Analysis (EPH1026)

courses: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory

core: Public health foundations, determinants and epidemiology: Health, Health Determinants and the European Union, and Demography and Epidemiology of Ageing and Migration, which teach the concepts of health and public health, determinants and socio-economic health inequalities, demography and epidemiological methods applied to population ageing

Disease and health technology: Communicable and Non-communicable Diseases in the EU and WHO-Euro (infectious disease, antimicrobial resistance, cardiovascular disease, diabetes, cancer, mental health) and Health-Technological Innovation and EU Competencies (pharmaceuticals, medical devices, big data)

European Union institutions, law, politics and health policy: the EU treaties, institutions and decision-making taught in year 1, and Health Policies at EU Level and Global Health Europe, which teaches health policy making, actors, advocacy and evidence-informed policy in a multilevel EU setting

Comparing European health systems: (Public) Health Care Systems in the EU, which analyses and compares the organisation, financing, insurance, reform and governance of health systems through health-system frameworks

Research methods, statistics and evidence: the interwoven Specialized Competency Lines (epidemiology, research methodology, statistics), Introduction to Statistical Methods for Data Analysis, Introduction to Quantitative Research Methods (programme evaluation) and the Year 1 literature-review paper, covering qualitative and quantitative methods and critical use of evidence
Ethics and philosophy of public health: the ethical issues and dilemmas of public health in Europe in year 1 and the Philosophy of Public Health competency line across the three years
Independent research and thesis: the Thesis Proposal and the 30-EC Placement and Thesis, in which students conduct independent research on a public-health question
adjacent: Social and behavioural determinants of health: social determinants of health and disease, lifestyle (diet, exercise, tobacco) and work as determinants, health promotion and psychological perspectives, studied through a socio-ecological model in Lifestyle, Work and Health in the EU

Health communication and policy advocacy: the Policy Advocacy competency line, which teaches students to understand, critique and influence public policy, and the programme's aim to develop skills in communication and policy advocacy

Environment, climate and sustainable health: the environment as a determinant of health (climate change, air and water quality, biodiversity, food supply) and sustainability in Healthy Environments and Sustainability in the EU
questions: How can European countries and the EU jointly address cross-border public-health threats such as pandemics, climate change, health inequities and ageing populations?
How do health systems, policies and outcomes compare across European countries?

trace: examines market failure, public goods, externalities, taxation, public spending, redistribution and political economy with empirical evidence on efficiency and equity; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the financing, market and sustainable-funding questions of the target's health-systems module, without covering health systems
Uses behavioural experiments and economic models to examine how framing, heuristics and bias affect decisions. These methods inform behavioural questions relevant to health.
Uses market research and consumer journeys to develop communication and engagement strategies. These methods complement audience analysis in health communication.

teaches research design, sampling and descriptive and inferential statistics (central tendency, spread, association, univariate and bivariate tests and analysis of variance); it directly implements the target's introductory statistics and research-methodology training and is the formal prerequisite of Public Economics

examines the psychological, social and structural dynamics within organisations; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the work and workplace dimension of the target's Lifestyle, Work and Health in the EU, without covering occupational health

develops data cleaning, manipulation and visualisation and an own data-analysis research project; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the target's work with real-world health data in its statistics and quantitative-methods modules

examines how sustainability policies are made and enforced, which actors shape them and what makes policy effective; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the sustainable-policy and governance questions of the target's Healthy Environments and Sustainability in the EU, without health content

covers the drivers and impacts of climate change, including effects on food production, health and migration, and climate governance and justice; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the climate-and-health strand of the target's Healthy Environments and Sustainability in the EU, but treats health only as one of several impacts

surveys legal systems and the main fields of law (constitutional, administrative, international, criminal and human-rights law and property, contract and tort law) and is the formal prerequisite of Foundations of European Union Law; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the legal grounding of the target's health-law and EU-treaty content without teaching health law

introduces the EU institutional framework, legal order, internal market, fundamental rights and free movement; it directly implements the EU treaties, institutions and legal structures taught in the target's Health, Health Determinants and the European Union, without any health-law content

teaches the main ethical theories and practical ethics (equality, responsibility, future generations and climate change); it makes a specific complementary contribution to the ethical dilemmas of public health studied in the target, although it is not a public-health ethics course

teaches the analytical tools for comparing political systems with theory-driven qualitative and quantitative research; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the comparative approach of the target's health-systems and policy modules, without covering health systems

teaches EU actors, institutions, decision-making rules and how state and non-state interests turn preferences into policy; it directly implements the political side of the target's Health Policies at EU Level and of the EU-institutions content of year 1, without any health focus

introduces sociological concepts, methods and theories for analysing social institutions and inequality; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the social determinants and socio-economic inequalities of health studied in the target, but does not itself treat health

teaches the design and conduct of qualitative research (interviews, meaning, power dynamics and data analysis in small-team projects); it directly implements the qualitative strand of the target's research-methodology training, here applied to social rather than health questions

covers social movement theories, environmental justice and civic engagement; it makes a specific complementary contribution to public-health advocacy and to the equity and environmental-justice dimensions of the target's determinants content

examines solidarity, social capital, social trust and civil society in modern societies; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the social-context determinants of health, although it does not treat health

introduces epidemiology as the science behind public health: how to study disease, risk and change over time and how to evaluate evidence for public-health decisions; it directly implements the epidemiology taught in the target's Demography and Epidemiology of Ageing and Migration and its epidemiology competency line, without the European or demographic focus

teaches drug origin, pharmacokinetics, therapeutic use and toxicity and the principles of rational drug development; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the pharmaceutical strand of the target's Health-Technological Innovation and EU Competencies, without the regulatory, policy or medical-device content

teaches the immune response, host-pathogen interaction and microbial strategies that circumvent host resistance; it directly implements the biological side of the infectious-disease content of the target's Communicable and Non-communicable Diseases module, but not its epidemiology, policy or antimicrobial-resistance policy frames

teaches the mechanisms of disease for the cardiovascular, lung, kidney, digestive, endocrine and nervous systems; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the non-communicable-disease content (cardiovascular disease, diabetes) of the target's Communicable and Non-communicable Diseases module, from a biomedical rather than population perspective

deepens cognitive neuroscience on memory, emotion, social cognition, attention and decision making and how to evaluate experimental research; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the individual-level psychological processes behind health behaviour

gives the cellular, molecular, genetic and systems-level foundations of health and biomedicine and is the formal prerequisite of Infection & Immunity, Mechanisms of Disease and Pharmacology; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the biological understanding of disease assumed by the target's disease and health-technology modules

introduces the study of brain and behaviour and is the formal prerequisite of Medical & Health Psychology, Advanced Research Seminar and Lifespan Developmental Psychology; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the psychological understanding of behaviour that underlies the target's lifestyle and psychological determinants of health

covers how feelings, thoughts and behaviour are shaped by attitudes, social influence and groups; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the psychological and social influences on health behaviour studied in the target, without applying them to health

teaches multivariate statistical models (regression, logistic regression, factor analysis, ANOVA/ANCOVA) and non-parametric tests; it directly implements the intermediate quantitative analysis taught in the target's Introduction to Quantitative Research Methods and competency lines, with psychological rather than health data

explores mental health and mental disorders across the lifespan from a bio-psycho-social perspective, including prevalence, development and the role of culture, gender and environment; it directly implements the mental-health strand of the target's non-communicable-disease content, from a clinical-psychology perspective

examines the bio-psycho-social approach to health and illness, health psychology theories and behaviour-related interventions in medical settings; it directly implements the health-behaviour and psychological-determinants content of the target's Lifestyle, Work and Health in the EU, without the European policy or occupational-health dimension
Develops evidence appraisal through systematic review protocols, literature searching, inclusion criteria and evidence synthesis.

follows human physical, cognitive and social development across the lifespan, including ageing; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the ageing-population focus of the target's Demography and Epidemiology of Ageing and Migration, from a developmental rather than demographic or epidemiological perspective

teaches classical rhetoric and argumentation and the analysis of persuasive discourse in politics, media and advertising; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the communication and advocacy skills the target develops, and is the foundation of Persuasive Communication

is a practice-based community-engaged course on public persuasion and debate in which students coach primary-school children; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the practice of public advocacy and communication, but has no health content

teaches persuasion strategies, framing, nudging and the ethics of persuasion, including sustainability and science messaging; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the communication and advocacy skills the target develops, without any health content

alternatives.label: European Public Health, Disease and Policy
alternatives.labelReason: Epidemiology, infection and disease, health psychology, research methods and EU law and politics form the closest academic option.
alternatives.concept: Study how disease and health risks are distributed and how public institutions respond. Combine epidemiology and biomedical science with health psychology, research methods, European law and policymaking.
progression: The biomedicine and law gateways precede dependent courses. Research methods and introductory statistics precede advanced evidence appraisal.

alternatives.label: Health Behaviour, Psychology and Communication
alternatives.labelReason: Health psychology, social behaviour, mental health and persuasive communication frame this related option.
alternatives.concept: Study how social conditions and individual behaviour affect health. Combine health psychology, sociology, behavioural economics and communication to examine health messages and the choices people make.
alternatives.distinctness: This option adds social and organisational psychology, mental health, behavioural economics and practical communication. The closest option gives greater weight to disease mechanisms, EU law and environmental governance.
traceOverrides: introduces epidemiology as the science of studying disease, risk and change over time and of evaluating evidence; in this programme it directly implements the epidemiological method with which behavioural and social risk factors are identified, and is the population-level anchor of the programme

teaches systematic reviews and meta-analysis in R for evidence-based policy making; in this programme it directly implements the evidence-synthesis training used to appraise behavioural and communication interventions and is placed last as the research capstone

teaches how state and non-state interests are turned into policy, the institutions and decision-making rules of the EU; in this programme it directly implements the political process behind the policy-advocacy strand, without any health focus

follows human development across the lifespan, including ageing; in this programme it makes a specific complementary contribution to the psychological and social determinants of health over the life course

teaches persuasion strategies, framing, nudging and the ethics of persuasion beyond the humanities in communication studies and social psychology; in this programme it makes a specific complementary contribution to health communication and advocacy as the capstone of the rhetoric sequence, without health content
progression: Psychology foundations precede advanced psychological study. Introductory rhetoric precedes practical rhetoric and persuasion. Behavioral Economics is placed in an available term before the final semester.

Field placement in a health organisation

selection.assessment: Two coherent options address the degree’s main themes. The closest combines epidemiology and disease with EU institutions and methods. The second emphasises behaviour, social determinants and communication. Climate science, governance and ecological study provide environmental context, but a separate option would have limited environmental epidemiology and exposure assessment. Business and economics contribute to organisational and funding questions without a sustained healthcare-management sequence. Placement and thesis are a required research format at Maastricht and do not generate a separate UCR curriculum.

blocks: Epidemiology, research methods, statistics and evidence

Epidemiology & Public Health teaches epidemiology as the science of studying disease, risk and change over time and of evaluating evidence, the core of Demography and Epidemiology of Ageing and Migration (epidemiological concepts and methods, research designs, association measures, bias and causal interpretation); it lacks the demography, ageing and migration topics and the EU focus.
Both use descriptive and inferential statistics. UCR applies study design and statistical analysis in a team project.

Statistics & Experimental Methods covers multivariate models (regression, logistic regression, ANOVA) and experimental design, the statistical-analysis and study-design part of Introduction to Quantitative Research Methods (chi-square tests, t-tests, regression and trial designs); it does not cover programme evaluation or process evaluation.

Advanced Research Seminar teaches systematic reviews and meta-analysis for evidence-based policy, the evidence-synthesis skill at the centre of the Year 1 literature-review paper (finding, interpreting and combining public-health evidence); it is a statistical synthesis course and does not teach academic writing.

Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: Epidemiology/Methodology/Policy Advocacy/Statistics 1 is a short introductory line interwoven with Health, Health Determinants and the European Union and introducing epidemiology, statistics and policy advocacy together; the relevant UCR methods courses are each aligned with a larger component and no scheduled UCR course addresses the policy-advocacy strand.

Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: Epidemiology/Methodology/Policy Advocacy/Statistics 2 is a short competency line interwoven with the disease module, combining epidemiology, methods, statistics and policy advocacy; no scheduled UCR course is a sufficiently direct counterpart that is not already aligned with a larger component.

Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: Epidemiology/Methodology/Policy Advocacy/Statistics 3 is a short competency line interwoven with the environment module; no scheduled UCR course is a sufficiently direct counterpart that is not already aligned with a larger component.

Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: Epidemiology/Methodology/Policy Advocacy/Statistics 4 is a short competency line interwoven with the health-technology module; no scheduled UCR course is a sufficiently direct counterpart that is not already aligned with a larger component.

Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: Epidemiology/Methodology/Policy Advocacy/Statistics 5 is a short competency line interwoven with the ageing and migration course; no scheduled UCR course is a sufficiently direct counterpart that is not already aligned with a larger component.

Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: Epidemiology/Methodology/Policy Advocacy/Statistics 6 is a short competency line interwoven with the lifestyle, work and health course; no scheduled UCR course is a sufficiently direct counterpart that is not already aligned with a larger component.

Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: Epidemiology/Methodology/Policy Advocacy/Statistics 7 is a short competency line interwoven with the health-systems course; no scheduled UCR course is a sufficiently direct counterpart that is not already aligned with a larger component.

Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: Epidemiology/Methodology/Policy Advocacy/Statistics 8 is a short competency line interwoven with the EU health-policy course; no scheduled UCR course is a sufficiently direct counterpart that is not already aligned with a larger component.

Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: Thesis Proposal is writing the research proposal for the bachelor thesis under supervision; UCR has no course for preparing an own thesis proposal, and Advanced Research Seminar is aligned with the literature-review component, so the relationship would be generic research training.

Infection & Immunity covers host-pathogen interaction, microbial resistance strategies and the immune response, the infectious-disease half of Communicable and Non-communicable Diseases in the EU and WHO-Euro; it does not cover its policy frames, non-communicable diseases or epidemiology.

Pharmacology covers drug origin, therapeutic use, toxicity and rational drug development, the pharmaceutical innovation strand of Health-Technological Innovation and EU Competencies; it does not cover medical devices, big data, safety assessment or the EU regulatory competencies.
Behaviour, psychology and social determinants of health

Medical & Health Psychology covers the bio-psycho-social approach to health and illness, health-psychology theory and interventions, matching the individual health-behaviour and intervention content of Lifestyle, Work and Health in the EU; it does not cover work characteristics or EU lifestyle and occupational-health policy.
European Union law, politics, economics and health systems

Foundations of European Union Law covers the EU institutional framework, legal order, fundamental rights and internal market, matching the EU history, treaties, institutions and legal-structures part of Health, Health Determinants and the European Union; it does not cover the concepts of health and public health, health determinants and health inequalities, which make up most of the component.

European Union Politics covers EU actors, institutions, decision-making rules and how interests are turned into policy, matching the multilevel EU policy-making, actors and advocacy of Health Policies at EU Level and Global Health Europe; it has no health-policy content or global-health dimension.

Public Economics covers market failure, public goods, externalities, taxation, public spending and redistribution, matching the financing and market part of (Public) Health Care Systems in the EU; it does not cover health-system frameworks, insurance schemes or health-system reforms.

Climate Change covers the drivers and societal impacts of climate change, including effects on health, food and migration, matching the climate-change part of Healthy Environments and Sustainability in the EU; it does not cover air and water quality, built environments or the health-environment policy focus.

Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: Philosophy of Public Health part 1 is a short competency line on the philosophical foundations of public health taught within the year 1 modules; Ethics teaches general moral theory and practical ethics, which is contextual rather than a direct counterpart to the philosophy of public health.

Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: Philosophy of Public Health part 2 is a short competency line on the philosophy of public health; Ethics is general moral theory and no UCR course teaches the philosophy of public health or of expertise and public participation.

Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: Philosophy of Public Health part 3 is a short competency line on topics such as public participation and the nature of expertise and knowledge in public health; no scheduled UCR course addresses these topics directly.
Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: Philosophy of Public Health part 4 is a short competency line on the philosophy of public health; no scheduled UCR course addresses its topics directly.
Excursion, year 2 paper, minor and placement with thesis
If the excursion is omitted, Maastricht adds its 1 EC to Lifestyle, Work and Health.

Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: the Year 2 Paper is an individual assignment on one of the four main content modules; no scheduled UCR course is a counterpart to this programme-specific paper.
The approved 30 EC minor can be taken at Maastricht or another institution. Its subject remains open.
Maastricht requires supervised placement research and an individual thesis. UCR displays optional independent research alongside it.

notes.text: The Bachelor European Public Health combines public health epidemiology, health policy and law in the European Union, health systems and health technology with a programme-wide methods line and a placement with thesis. At UCR, students can approach public health through fields such as epidemiology, biomedicine, health psychology, sociology, EU law and politics and sustainability. These programmes therefore offer related perspectives rather than reproducing a full public health curriculum.

The Bachelor European Public Health includes a more extensive sequence in European health policy, health systems and health law, environmental health and health technology. At UCR, students can study epidemiology, disease, EU law and politics and sustainability, but UCR does not offer the same depth or sequence in public health.

audience.programmeDescription: Maastricht studies health, disease and healthcare across Europe. The programme combines epidemiology and research methods with health systems, public policy, ethics and a supervised research placement.
audience.comparisonExplanation: The closest UCR option combines disease and epidemiology with research methods, EU law and politics. The second explores the social and behavioural factors that affect health and how public messages reach people. Maastricht has dedicated courses in European health systems and a required placement and thesis.

curriculum.limitation: This comparison follows the standard programme. The approved minor remains open.
